newsitem.title: UK: Insurance cycle turned down in 1996, says UK's ABI.
newsitem.headline: Insurance cycle turned down in 1996, says UK's ABI.

text.p: The Association of British Insurers (ABI) on Wednesday revealed a mixed performance by the industry in 1996, with falling profits in general insurance but a record year in life and pensions business.
While prospects for life insurance remained bright, the ABI warned that last year was likely to mark the downturn in the general insurance cycle.
UK insurance companies' world-wide general insurance trading profit was down 29 percent from 1995 at three billion pounds ($4.9 billion), its lowest level since 1993.
The major cause of the reversal was a sharp deterioration in underwriting losses, which virtually tripled to nearly 1.9 billion pounds in 1996.
All main areas of business produced worse underwriting results, with motor insurance particularly bad, said the ABI.

"After four years of improving trading results, both in absolute terms and as a percentage of premiums, 1996 looks to be the turning point in the infamous insurance cycle," said ABI director general Mark Boleat.
"Further pressure on profits can be expected this year, with strong competition for business and higher claims in a number of important areas."
In the UK, motor insurance underwriting losses jumped to 633 million pounds from 80 million, as a result of both an increase in claims and lower premiums.
Premium income remained steady, reflecting continuing competitiveness and the reluctance of some companies to increase rates and risk losing market share.
However, the beginning of 1997 had seen increases in some rates and these look set to continue according to the ABI.
Non-motor underwriting profit was more than halved to 173 million pounds from 421 million, with severe competition and rising claims for fire and weather taking a toll.
"Our members paid out on over 200,000 claims for burst pipes alone, with the bill for cold weather damage exceeding 400 million pounds," said the ABI's deputy director general Tony Baker.
The high level of subsidence claims was another factor and 1997 first quarter claims, which rose 22 percent to 83 million pounds, suggested this was likely to continue, he added.

Marine, aviation and transport insurance (MAT) reversed an underwriting profit of 29 million pounds to a 52 million pound loss, while the non-MAT reinsurance account loss quadrupled to 263 million pounds.
Motor underwriting losses in the U.S. increased to 67 million pounds as did non-motor to 424 million pounds from 281 million last year.
In contrast, world-wide net long term life and pensions premium income rose 18 percent to a record 66.4 billion pounds in 1996.
Single premium business had a particularly good year, with its flexibility and lower costs encouraging strong growth.
In the UK, the increase was 17 percent to 52.7 billion pounds, with all sectors except industrial branch showing rises.
Life insurance premiums also rose 17 percent to 24.4 billion pounds within which single premiums increased 37 percent to 12.4 billion pounds.
Pensions rose 16 percent to 25.6 billion pounds, with single premiums up 29 percent to 15.3 billion pounds.
Overseas premiums increased 21 percent to 13.7 billion pounds.
